final_answer:
Based on the provided evidence, **Traffic Patterns** achieved the highest detection rate against C2 channels running on trusted services. The specific indicator within this tier was **JA4 fingerprints**, which achieved a **100% detection rate**. 

The evidence states that while Reputation-based detection failed to identify any channels and Beacon Detection was only marginally viable (2/4), Traffic Patterns proved most viable. Specifically, it notes that "Structural and behavioral indicators, such as TLS session resumption and JA4 fingerprinting, outperform reputation in detecting trusted service abuse" and identifies JA4 fingerprints as having "100% detection" [c4].

citations.title: Network Artifacts of Trusted Service Abuse (page 1)
citations.snippet: sing 51 packet captures (3 baselines, 6 automated browser tests and 6 framework tests per service). Across four detection tiers, Reputation-based detection failed to identify any C2 channels; Beacon Detection was marginally viable when using clustering (2/4); Traffic Metadata was partially viable, with mixed results other than JA4 fingerprints (100% detection); and Traffic Patterns proved most viable, with both TLS session resumption near-zero (vs 22%+ for browser) and a 2.6x upload/download ratio gap (1.41 vs 0.55 means). Structural and behavioral indicators, such as TLS session resumption and JA4 fingerprinting, outperform reputation in detecting trusted service abuse.

documents.title: Network Artifacts of Trusted Service Abuse (page 27)
documents.snippet: Network Artifacts of Trusted Service Abuse 27 Nicholas Vaniscak, vaniscak.nicholas@gmail.com tested four publicly available C2 frameworks that operate over trusted services, Discord, Dropbox, Gmail, and OneNote, and found that both reputation-based detection and traditional beacon detection are ineffective at detecting their abuse (Patsakis, Arroyo, & Casino, 2024).
